1. verus! {
2. 
3. //==================================================================================================
4. // TableIndex — a validated page-table slot number
5. //==================================================================================================
6. 
7. // A `TableIndex` carries exactly one piece of caller-visible information: the validated index
8. // value. Its abstract value is a single `nat` (see `view_design.md`).
9. impl View for TableIndex {
10.     type V = nat;
11. 
12.     // `closed`: callers reference `self@` and the in-range invariant; the mapping to the inner
13.     // `usize` field is hidden. The abstract value is "the validated slot number".
14.     closed spec fn view(&self) -> nat {
15.         self.0 as nat
16.     }
17. }
18. 
19. impl TableIndex {
20.     // The validated-range guarantee every caller depends on: a `TableIndex` is always a legal
21.     // slot. Enforced as a type invariant so the bound holds unconditionally for any value callers
22.     // hold — this is exactly what keeps `read`/`write` (and `gva.rs`'s `checked_mul`) within one
23.     // page, and is established once at each construction site (`new`, `pd_index`, `pt_index`).
24.     #[verifier::type_invariant]
25.     pub open spec fn inv(&self) -> bool {
26.         self@ < crate::mem::PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH
27.     }
28. }
29. 
30. //==================================================================================================
31. // Virtual-address index extraction (pure helpers)
32. //==================================================================================================
33. 
34. // Low `log2(PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH)` bits of `vaddr >> shift`. Mirrors the exec masking
35. // `(vaddr >> shift) & (PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH - 1)` exactly; the mask makes the result `< LEN`.
36. pub open spec fn spec_table_index(vaddr: usize, shift: usize) -> nat {
37.     ((vaddr >> shift) & ((crate::mem::PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH - 1) as usize)) as nat
38. }
39. 
40. // PD index = bits [PGTAB_SHIFT, PGTAB_SHIFT + log2(LEN)) of `vaddr`.
41. pub open spec fn spec_pd_index(vaddr: usize) -> nat {
42.     spec_table_index(vaddr, crate::mem::PGTAB_SHIFT)
43. }
44. 
45. // PT index = bits [PAGE_SHIFT, PAGE_SHIFT + log2(LEN)) of `vaddr`.
46. pub open spec fn spec_pt_index(vaddr: usize) -> nat {
47.     spec_table_index(vaddr, crate::mem::PAGE_SHIFT)
48. }
49. 
50. //==================================================================================================
51. // TableEntry codec (the per-entry round-trip law)
52. //==================================================================================================
53. 
54. // Abstract serialization / decoding of a `TableEntry`. These mirror the exec `raw` / `from_raw`
55. // trait methods. They are deliberately *unbounded* over `E` (no `TableEntry` bound) to avoid a
56. // definitional cycle (`TableEntry`'s method specs reference these, so a bound here would make the
57. // trait depend on a function that depends on the trait).
58. //
59. // `spec_entry_from_raw` returns `None` for a word that is not a valid encoding of `E` — exactly
60. // the `read` failure path callers map to `InvalidArgument` (see `caller_analysis.md`).
61. pub uninterp spec fn spec_entry_raw<E>(e: E) -> PteWord;
62. 
63. pub uninterp spec fn spec_entry_from_raw<E>(w: PteWord) -> Option<E>;
64. 
65. //==================================================================================================
66. // Global ghost model of page-table memory
67. //==================================================================================================
68. 
69. // Page-table memory is volatile, caller-owned storage the `Table<E>` handle does not contain
70. // (the struct holds only `base`). It is modeled here as a *global, parameter-free* ghost
71. // function — the same device used for the physical-frame subsystem (`mm::phys::phys_view()`):
72. // the abstract state is named globally rather than threaded through a permission parameter, so
73. // `read`/`write` keep their exec signatures and do not cascade ghost arguments into out-of-scope
74. // callers (`identity_map::ensure_pt`/`ensure_pte`/`identity_map_page`).
75. //
76. // `spec_table_word(addr, index)` is the raw word currently stored at slot `index` of the
77. // page-table page based at `addr`. Because it is a pure function, a call to `write` only updates
78. // knowledge about the *one* slot named in its `ensures`; every other slot/page is automatically
79. // preserved across the call (the caller-facing frame condition). The cross-call write transition
80. // (and its consistency when the same slot is written twice) is realized in the proving phase by a
81. // ghost token over the page-table pages — exactly the `phys_view()` "transition realized in the
82. // proving phase" placeholder.
83. pub uninterp spec fn spec_table_word(addr: nat, index: nat) -> PteWord;
84. 
85. // The decoded entry currently stored at slot `index` of the page based at `addr`: the value a
86. // `read` returns. This is the `index -> Option<E>` entry map from `view_design.md`, expressed
87. // pointwise over the global word store.
88. pub open spec fn spec_table_read<E>(addr: nat, index: nat) -> Option<E> {
89.     spec_entry_from_raw::<E>(spec_table_word(addr, index))
90. }
91. 
92. //==================================================================================================
93. // Table<E> — a typed, non-owning handle over one page-table page
94. //==================================================================================================
95.

97. // address (see `view_design.md`): its caller-meaningful identity is *which page* read/write act
98. // on (`addr`), and its observable contents are the per-slot decoded entry map (`entries`). The
99. // contents live in volatile, caller-owned memory the struct does not store, so the view reads
100. // them from the global `spec_table_read` ghost rather than from struct fields.
101. pub struct TableView<E> {
102.     /// Physical/identity-mapped base address this handle denotes.
103.     pub addr: nat,
104.     /// Decoded entry at each valid slot — `entries[i]` is what `read(i)` returns
105.     /// (`None` = the slot holds a word that is not a valid encoding of `E`).
106.     pub entries: Map<nat, Option<E>>,
107. }
108. 
109. impl<E: TableEntry> View for Table<E> {
110.     type V = TableView<E>;
111. 
112.     closed spec fn view(&self) -> TableView<E> {
113.         TableView {
114.             addr: self.base as nat,
115.             entries: Map::new(
116.                 |i: nat| i < crate::mem::PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH,
117.                 |i: nat| spec_table_read::<E>(self.base as nat, i),
118.             ),
119.         }
120.     }
121. }
122.

21.         ensures ret == x + 1,
22.     { x + 1 }
23. } // verus!
24. 
25. // ❌ WRONG — attribute style
26. #[verus_spec(ret => requires x < 100, ensures ret == x + 1)]
27. fn foo(x: u32) -> u32 { x + 1 }
28. ```
29. 
30. Even if existing code uses attribute style, write all new code in `verus! { }` style.
31. Attribute style is less mature; `verus! { }` can be auto-converted later.
32. 
33. ## Source Integrity (exec code)
34. 
35. The following rules apply to the original source files (e.g. `lib.rs`), not to
36. `*.spec.rs` / `*.proof.rs` which are freely editable.
37. 
38. Verus verification is **in-place**: specs and proofs are added directly alongside
39. exec code. The annotated code remains fully compilable and runnable — Verus
40. constructs are erased during normal `cargo build` via cfg-gating. Do not change
41. code logic; keep changes minimal so developers can review diffs easily.
42. 
43. **Preserve:** exec logic, function signatures, struct definitions, comments,
44. debug assertions, and all other existing code. If a construct is unsupported by
45. Verus (e.g. `debug_assert!`), cfg-gate it with `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]`
46. rather than deleting.
47. 
48. **Never cfg-gate away exec functions or impl blocks.** Adding
49. `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` to an entire function/impl and providing a
50. verus-annotated copy is forbidden — it verifies the copy, not the real code,
51. and the two will silently diverge. Contracts must be added to the original
52. function in-place.
53.

55. proof blocks, assert), vstd imports (cfg-gated), named returns `-> (ret: T)`,
56. ghost/tracked variables, `#[cfg_attr(not(verus_keep_ghost), derive(...))]` gating.
57.

59. only if Verus genuinely cannot express a construct — first search vstd for
60. alternatives, build a minimal reproducer proving unsupported, then make the
61. smallest change needed and document why.
62.

64. source integrity. Fix all inconsistencies. For unavoidable ones, you must

73. | `assume(...)` | Banned |

94.

98. maps, arithmetic, pointers, atomics).

102. - **Don't hallucinate syntax** — when unsure, check the Verus reference or vstd examples.
103.

107.

109. 2. Search verified dependency specs for reusable `assume_specification`

112.

114. non-`verus!{}` constants, complex control flow — all handleable via the
115. steps above.
116. 
117. Partial contracts are always better than none. If 1 out of 5 clauses is
118. inexpressible, write the other 4.

3. description: "Proving methodology and mindset for Verus verification: function-by-function approach, persistence through failures, clean verification, and bug reporting. Use when writing proofs or resolving verification failures."

6. # Proving Guide
7. 
8. Read `verus-constraints` first. Study `docs/examples/binary-search/proof/`
9. for a working example.
10. 
11. ## Core Approach
12. 
13. 1. **One function at a time.** Resolve `admit()` function by function. Do not
14.    move to the next function until the current one verifies cleanly.
15. 
16. 2. **Keep trying.** When verification fails, read the error log carefully,
17.    try a different proof strategy, and iterate. You are capable of solving
18.    this — if one approach fails, try the next. Do not give up or ask for
19.    suggestions; work through possible approaches systematically.
20. 
21. 3. **Report genuine bugs.** If after thorough attempts you determine the
22.    failure is caused by a code bug (not a proof gap), report it immediately
23.    using the `bug-reporting` skill. Do not silently work around code bugs.
24. 
25. 4. **Clean verification.** After all proofs pass, check for warnings and
26.    resolve them. A clean verification has zero errors AND zero warnings.
27. 
28. ## Verification Tool
29. 
30. Use `make verify-<crate> MODULE=<module>` to verify the current module during
31. proving. After all modules are done, run `make verify-<crate>` (no MODULE) to
32. confirm the full crate still passes. The output includes:
33. - **Verification result** — pass/fail with error details
34. - **Cheating detection** — flags `admit`, `assume`, `external_body`, `trusted`;
35.   all cheating must be resolved before the proof is considered complete
36. - **Coverage** — which functions have contracts
37. 
38. After verification passes, use the `ast-consistency` skill to check that
39. exec code was not accidentally modified during proving. Fix all
40. inconsistencies before finalizing.
41.

 # Proving Guide
 
 Read `verus-constraints` first. Study `docs/examples/binary-search/proof/`
 for a working example.
 
 ## Core Approach
 
 1. **One function at a time.** Resolve `admit()` function by function. Do not
    move to the next function until the current one verifies cleanly.
 
 2. **Keep trying.** When verification fails, read the error log carefully,
    try a different proof strategy, and iterate. You are capable of solving
    this — if one approach fails, try the next. Do not give up or ask for
    suggestions; work through possible approaches systematically.
 
 3. **Report genuine bugs.** If after thorough attempts you determine the
    failure is caused by a code bug (not a proof gap), report it immediately
    using the `bug-reporting` skill. Do not silently work around code bugs.
 
 4. **Clean verification.** After all proofs pass, check for warnings and
    resolve them. A clean verification has zero errors AND zero warnings.
 
 ## Verification Tool
 
 Use `make verify-<crate> MODULE=<module>` to verify the current module during
 proving. After all modules are done, run `make verify-<crate>` (no MODULE) to
 confirm the full crate still passes. The output includes:
 - **Verification result** — pass/fail with error details
 - **Cheating detection** — flags `admit`, `assume`, `external_body`, `trusted`;
   all cheating must be resolved before the proof is considered complete
 - **Coverage** — which functions have contracts
 
 After verification passes, use the `ast-consistency` skill to check that
 exec code was not accidentally modified during proving. Fix all
 inconsistencies before finalizing.

  `v -> v'` deferral convention in `identity_map.spec.rs`.

# Verus-Unsupported Constructs — `arch::x86::mem::paging::table`

This file records language/library constructs in the `table` module that Verus
cannot translate or verify, together with the minimal reproduction and the
trust-boundary mitigation used.

## 1. Integer-to-pointer cast (`usize as *const T` / `usize as *mut T`)

### Where
- `Table::<E>::read` — `let ptr: *const PteWord = (self.base + offset) as *const PteWord;`
- `Table::<E>::write` — `let ptr: *mut PteWord = (self.base + offset) as *mut PteWord;`

Both functions materialize a raw pointer to a hardware page-table slot from the
integer base address stored in `self.base`, then perform a volatile load/store.

### Minimal reproduction
```rust
use vstd::prelude::*;
#[verus_spec]
pub fn load(base: usize) -> u32 {
    let ptr: *const u32 = base as *const u32;
    unsafe { ::core::ptr::read_volatile(ptr) }
}
```

### Exact error
```
error: Verus does not support this cast: `usize` to `*const u32`
 --> vt_cast.rs:5:27
  |
5 |     let ptr: *const u32 = base as *const u32;
  |                           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
```

### Why it is unsupported
Verus has no model for int-to-pointer provenance / materialization. A verified
load or store requires a `PointsTo`-style permission token witnessing ownership
of the target bytes; an `usize`-derived pointer to externally-owned, volatile
MMIO/page-table memory has no such token in scope.

### Mitigation (trust boundary)
`read` and `write` are marked `#[verus_verify(external_body)]` and recorded in
`verus-ai-logs/tcb-allowed.md`. This is the same int-to-pointer boundary already
used by `bump_allocator::alloc` (`usize as *mut`) and `frame::instance`. Their
`requires`/`ensures` describe the abstract contract; the bodies (the cast + the
volatile access) are trusted.

### Deferred work
`read` carries its **full** abstract contract: the global page-table-memory ghost
`spec_table_word` / `spec_table_read::<E>` models the slot contents
(parameter-free, like `phys_view()`), so `read` ensures
`result == spec_table_read::<E>(self@.addr, index@)`. `write` carries only the
sound `requires index@ < PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH` and **no** contents `ensures`: pinning
the *pure* `spec_table_word` cell to the caller-chosen `entry` in an assumed
(`external_body`) postcondition is unsound — two writes of distinct entries to the
same slot derive `spec_entry_raw(e1) == spec_entry_raw(e2)`, and with
`lemma_entry_roundtrip` that gives `e1 == e2`, i.e. `false` (Turn 2 review). The
genuine `old@ -> @` write transition (and its same-slot consistency) is therefore
deferred to a proving-phase ghost token over the page-table pages — the same
`phys_view()` / `identity_map_view()` placeholder rationale. Only the *body* (the
`usize`→pointer cast + the volatile access) is trusted via `external_body`. No exec
signature changed, so the out-of-scope `admit()` callers in `identity_map.rs`
(`ensure_pt`, `ensure_pte`, `identity_map_page`) do not cascade.
